extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers preparing for mathematical olympiads / problem-solvers in Euclidean geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Solutions, lemmas and locus/inequality results for Euclidean geometry problems aimed at olympiad-level problem solving. Contains many techniques (reflection, area methods, vector/centroid/orthocenter facts, Ptolemy, Ceva, loci) and worked examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection + parallelogram trick for distance inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: If O is arbitrary and M is midpoint of AB then |OA − OB| ≤ 2·OM. Reflect O across M to O' so AOBO' is a parallelogram; OA = BO'. Use triangle inequalities in triangle B O O' to get 2OM > |OA − OB|. If O on line AB, use coordinates and absolute value manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: reflect a point across the midpoint to create a parallelogram, then apply triangle inequalities or coordinate algebra. Equality case discussed (O on segment AB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of altitudes < perimeter
rubrics_metrics.description: In any triangle, the sum of the lengths of the altitudes is less than the triangle's perimeter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof technique: reduce to right triangle fact 'leg < hypotenuse' via reflections across vertices; compare each altitude to the adjacent side (AA' ≤ AB etc.) and add. Note the inequality is strict because at most one angle can be right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounds for sum of distances from interior point to vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: For triangle with perimeter P and M interior point, P/2 < MA + MB + MC < P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower bound: sum pairwise inequalities MA+MB > AB etc. (add); Upper bound: use known inequality MB+MC < AB+AC etc. (Problem 2.3) and add cyclically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of medians inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: If A', B', C' are midpoints of sides, then (3/4)P < AA' + BB' + CC' < P (where P is perimeter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use centroid G: GA+GB+GC > P/2 from previous problem, and centroid divides each median in ratio 1:2 (AA' = 3/2 GA), so AA'+BB'+CC' = 3/2(GA+GB+GC) > 3/4 P. Upper bound follows by triangle inequality (see Problem 2.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using diagonal intersection and triangle inequalities in quadrilaterals
rubrics_metrics.description: In convex quadrilateral ABCD, from AB + BD ≤ AC + CD one can deduce AB < AC by considering intersection O of diagonals and applying triangle inequalities AB < AO + OB, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: insert intersection point of diagonals, write triangle inequalities for pairs of triangles sharing segments, combine to compare side lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal-length matching yields non-crossing segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Given n red and n blue points (no three collinear), a pairing of red to blue points that minimizes total length has no intersecting segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two segments AB and CD cross, replacing them by AC and BD shortens total length (by triangle inequality variant), contradicting minimality. Use this to assert existence of noncrossing perfect matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial shooting problem principles (odd n survival)
rubrics_metrics.description: With n odd and distinct pairwise distances, when each gunman shoots his nearest neighbor, at least one gunman survives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a closest pair; they shoot each other. If any other shoots one of them, some other person must survive (count bullets). Remove the pair and iterate; oddness ensures someone survives in last triple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole-angle bound: indegree ≤ 5 for nearest-shooter graph
rubrics_metrics.description: No gunman is shot more than five times when each shoots his closest neighbor (with all pairwise distances distinct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If someone were shot ≥ 6 times, angles at that gunman have a sector ≤ 60°, producing a contradiction via triangle-angle side comparisons: if A1 and A2 are two shooters forming ≤60° at A, one of remaining angles in triangle A1AA2 exceeds 60° so side comparisons contradict nearest-neighbor assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonintersecting trajectories via segment-sum contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullet trajectories (segments from shooters to targets) cannot intersect under the nearest-neighbor rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If AB and CD intersect, then AB < AD and CD < BC, so AB + CD < AD + BC, contradicting appropriate minimality/nearest relations; hence segments do not cross.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medians of triangle can form a triangle (vector sum zero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Medians AA', BB', CC' of triangle ABC can be the side lengths of a triangle: AA' + BB' + CC' = 0 vectorially (their vector sum is zero), and they are non-collinear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: build parallelogram relations (see figure) to produce triangle with side lengths equal to medians; equivalently use vector identity AA' + BB' + CC' = 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection across a line minimizes broken-path length
rubrics_metrics.description: Given A and B on same side of line XY, the point M on XY minimizing AM + MB is intersection of XY with AB', the reflection of B across XY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflect B across line to B' and use straight-line shortest-path property: AM + MB = AM + MB' ≥ AB', with equality when M is intersection of AB' and XY.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perimeter-minimizing inscribed triangle is orthic triangle (acute case)
rubrics_metrics.description: For acute triangle ABC, points M∈BC, N∈CA, P∈AB minimizing perimeter of triangle MNP are feet of altitudes (orthic triangle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: reflect M across AB and AC to reduce minimizing perimeter to minimizing distance between two reflected points; similarity and fixed-angle arguments show minimum occurs when MA is altitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibonacci-type growth from triangle inequality obstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Given seven real numbers in (1,13), at least three are side lengths of a triangle; otherwise ordering and repeated application of 'if no triangle then small two sum ≤ next' yields Fibonacci-like growth forcing largest ≥ 13, contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: sort numbers and use inductive inequalities a3 ≥ a1 + a2 ≥ 2, etc., producing bounds a7 ≥ 13.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area-doubling reflection locus (ratio of triangle areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find locus of M with [ABM] = 2[ACM], reflect A across C to A' so that [AMC'] = 2[AMC]; locus of points with equal areas [ABM]=[AC' M] is union of a median and a line parallel to BC through A (specific result described).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General technique: convert area ratio conditions to equality of areas with a reflected point, then identify lines (medians or parallels) giving equal base*height.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area ratio equals side ratio: [ABM]/[ACM] = BD/CD when M on AD
rubrics_metrics.description: Let D on BC and M on AD; then [ABM]/[ACM] = BD/CD. Using this area ratio lemma one deduces Ceva's theorem: concurrent AD, BE, CF iff product BD/CD · CE/EA · AF/FB = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: express areas via base*height; eliminate common factors; use multiplicative chaining to derive Ceva.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal-area quadrilateral interior point -> diagonal bisects other diagonal
rubrics_metrics.description: If M inside convex quadrilateral ABCD satisfies [MAB]=[MBC]=[MCD]=[MDA], then one diagonal passes through midpoint of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: equal-area equalities imply M lies on medians of triangles sharing vertices; either medians coincide producing diagonal through midpoint, or M lies on one diagonal which bisects the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area-locus for linear combinations of triangle areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Given linear area relation like [MAB] + 2[MCD] = k, the locus of M in quadrilateral interior is a segment (possibly point or empty) determined by parallels/midpoints depending on k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine reflection/area-constant constructions (earlier problems) to reduce to finding points on a fixed line or segment; outcome depends on k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of distances to two non-parallel lines constant → rectangle locus
rubrics_metrics.description: Locus of points whose sum of distances to two non-parallel lines equals k is a rectangle whose diagonals are the two lines; in different angle sectors the locus is segment(s) parallel to given lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: convert distance sum to area constancy by fixing circle and using projections; consider each angle region separately to obtain segments; combining yields rectangle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoints of AC, BD, EF collinear (Newton line variant)
rubrics_metrics.description: In complete quadrilateral configuration of ABCD with E = AB∩CD and F = AD∩BC, the midpoints of AC, BD and EF are collinear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses area-locus ideas: find segment of interior points with certain half-area sum; show midpoints lie on same segment; alternative proof via parallelogram/lemma about equal-area parallelograms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of distances to sides constant implies parallelogram
rubrics_metrics.description: If for variable interior point of convex quadrilateral ABCD the sum of distances to the sides is constant then ABCD is a parallelogram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: consider small constant-width strips near sides, translate sum-of-area argument to conclude certain side pairs parallel, then deduce opposite angles equal, hence parallelogram. Also gives generalization to n-gons with weighted side-length identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altitudes of ABC are angle bisectors of triangle of feet DEF
rubrics_metrics.description: If D,E,F are feet of altitudes of ABC, then altitudes of ABC are angle bisectors of triangle DEF (i.e., BE bisects ∠DEF etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show certain quadrilaterals are cyclic (diameter arguments) and compare angles to obtain equal angles indicating bisectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ptolemy's inequality and characterization of cyclic quadrilateral
rubrics_metrics.description: For convex quadrilateral, AD·BC + AB·CD ≥ AC·BD, with equality iff quadrilateral is cyclic (Ptolemy's theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct A' such that triangles ABD and A'BC are similar, derive equalities (5.1)-(5.2), sum them to get inequality; equality occurs when A' lies on AC i.e., when ∠ADB = ∠ACB (cyclic condition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three circumcircles of triangles with interior points concur
rubrics_metrics.description: Given A',B',C' points on BC,CA,AB respectively (interior), the circumcircles of AB'C', BA'C' and CA'B' have a common point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take intersection M of two such circumcircles and use cyclic quadrilateral angle equalities to show M belongs to the third; observation extends to some degenerate collinear cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthocenter vector lemma: OA + OB + OC = OH
rubrics_metrics.description: If H is orthocenter and O circumcenter of triangle ABC, then vector OA + OB + OC = OH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: choose A' such that AA' is diameter; parallelogram relations between A'BHC give H A + H B + H C = 2HO. Convert to O-based vectors to obtain OA+OB+OC=OH. Consequence: OH = 3·OG where G is centroid (OH = 3·OG).

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthocenters of four triangles in a cyclic quadrilateral form congruent quadrilateral
rubrics_metrics.description: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, orthocenters of triangles ABC, BCD, CDA, DAB are vertices of a quadrilateral congruent to ABCD; their centroids form a cyclic quadrilateral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use orthocenter vector lemma componentwise to show vector differences between orthocenters equal corresponding side vectors of ABCD. Centroids are homothetic images (ratio 1/3) of orthocenter quadrilateral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthocenters of midpoints-triangles form a parallelogram
rubrics_metrics.description: If K,L,M,N are midpoints of sides of cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, orthocenters of triangles AKN, BKL, CLM, DMN are vertices of a parallelogram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply orthocenter vector lemma and homothety arguments: OHA + OHC = OA+OB+OC+OD = OHB + OHD, giving equal midpoints of opposite orthocenter segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpendiculars from midpoints to opposite sides concur
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpendiculars from midpoints of sides of a cyclic quadrilateral to the opposite sides are concurrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: consider circumcenter O and show quadrilaterals OKXM and OLYN are parallelograms so midpoints of OX and OY coincide with midpoints of corresponding sides; deduce concurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projections of intersection of perpendicular diagonals form cyclic quadrilateral
rubrics_metrics.description: If diagonals AC and BD of convex quadrilateral intersect perpendicularly at O, then projections of O on the sides are vertices of a cyclic quadrilateral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let projections K,L,M,N on AB,BC,CD,DA respectively; sum angle equalities over the four right triangles to conclude opposite angle sum 180°, hence cyclic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational equiangular pentagon must be regular
rubrics_metrics.description: An equiangular pentagon with rational side lengths is regular (all sides equal); argument uses cos72° irrationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use isosceles triangle decompositions in equiangular pentagon to relate side differences to cos72°, then irrationality of cos72° forces equalities of corresponding sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime-sided equiangular polygon with rational sides is regular
rubrics_metrics.description: For prime p, any equiangular p-gon with rational side lengths is regular; conversely, if p composite there exist non-regular rational examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic method: consider polynomial P(X)=a1 + a2 X + ... + ap X^{p-1} with rational coefficients and ζ = e^{2π i/p}; since ζ also root of cyclotomic Q(X)=1+X+...+X^{p-1}, gcd arguments and Eisenstein criterion show P is constant multiple of Q, forcing equal sides when p prime; construction for composite p gives counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Odd equiangular cyclic polygon is regular
rubrics_metrics.description: An equiangular polygon with odd number of sides inscribed in a circle is regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congruence of successive triangles (sharing a side and equal angles) yields equality of many side pairs and propagates to all sides equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone side-lengths in equiangular polygon imply regular
rubrics_metrics.description: If an equiangular polygon has side lengths a1 ≥ a2 ≥ ... ≥ an then the polygon is regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric proof: project sides to a symmetry axis and compare projections showing equality forced; algebraic proof: consider polynomial P(X)=a1 + a2 X + ... and show any root α must have |α|≥1, with equality only when all ai equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equiangular rational octagon has center symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: An equiangular octagon with rational side lengths has a symmetry center (central symmetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 135° angles to relate sums of opposite side combinations involving √2/2; rationality forces simpler equalities AB=EF etc., implying opposite sides equal and parallel, creating parallelograms and a common midpoint (center).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inradius formula for right triangle and application
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma: In right triangle with legs y,z and hypotenuse x, inradius r = (y + z − x)/2. Applied to decompositions in equilateral triangle problems to compare sums of inradii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via tangency segments equalities; use lemma to transform inradius-sum identities into equalities of side-projection sums, then use parallel-projection arguments to complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incenter-centroid solvability implies equilateral triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: If for every point M on AB one can find N on BC and P on CA such that incenter I of triangle ABC is centroid of MNP, then ABC is equilateral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set barycentric ratios m,n,p and derive linear relations; require n,p in (0,1) for all m∈(0,1) forces special equalities that imply a=b=c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of interior K making triangle KLM equilateral ↔ ∠A = 60°
rubrics_metrics.description: Let L and M be internal angle-bisector feet from B and C respectively. There exists K on BC such that KLM is equilateral iff ∠A = 60°.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direction '⇒': use bisector and equal-length arguments to deduce ∠A = 60°. Direction '⇐': construct K with MK ⟂ BL and use cyclic/quadrilateral angle facts to show triangle is equilateral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polygon with 60°-realizer for every pair of vertices must be equilateral triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: If convex polygon P1...Pn has property: for any two vertices Pi,Pj there exists Pk with ∠PiPkPj = 60°, then polygon is an equilateral triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick minimal-length chord PiPj and corresponding equilateral triangle then compare with maximal equilateral triangle inscribed; convexity forces polygon to coincide with equilateral triangle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collinearity of points obtained from parallels through point on circumcircle
rubrics_metrics.description: For equilateral triangle ABC and point P on its circumcircle, draw parallels to BC, CA, AB through P meeting CA, AB, BC at M,N,P respectively; then M,N,P are collinear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove equality of certain angles via cyclic quadrilaterals constructed from parallels (use isosceles/trapezoid/cyclic arguments) to conclude collinearity (Simson-like line in equilateral case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Projections of arbitrary point onto three lines through circumcircle point form equilateral triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: If P on circumcircle of equilateral triangle ABC and Q arbitrary, the projections of Q onto lines PA, PB, PC are vertices of an equilateral triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cyclic quadrilateral properties (quadrilaterals formed by projection points, P and Q are cyclic) and angle equalities (120°/60° relations) to deduce all triangle angles are 60°.
